terms.grammar: ascendō, ascendere, ascendī, ascēnsum, with in + accusative
evidence: Cic. Sen. 34: in equum omnīnō nōn ascendere
terms.comment: Cicero’s phrase; Livy has equum ascendere with the plain accusative (Liv. 23.14, Lewis & Short). To get off is ex equō dēscendere (Cicero, below).

terms.grammar: cōnscendō, cōnscendere, cōnscendī, cōnscēnsum, with accusative
terms.comment: Livy and the poets; cōnscendere is chiefly to go on board a ship (see get on, of a bicycle).

terms.grammar: īnsiliō, īnsilīre, īnsiluī, with in + accusative

terms.gloss: dismount, jump down from a horse
terms.comment: Caesar’s Germans leap down to fight on foot.

phrases.latin: cum ingressus iter pedibus sit, in equum omnīnō nōn ascendere; cum autem equō, ex equō nōn dēscendere
phrases.english: once he has set out on foot, he never gets on a horse at all; once on horseback, he never gets off

phrases.latin: Deinde īnsilit in equum, indit pedēs stapedibus, sinistrā capessit lōrum (habēnam) frēnī
phrases.english: Then he jumps onto the horse, puts his feet in the stirrups and takes the rein of the bridle in his left hand

sources: Lewis & Short: ascendo · Lewis & Short: conscendo · Lewis & Short: insilio · Lewis & Short: desilio · Lewis & Short: descendo
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-comenius), checked against the editions named there.
Livy, Ovid and Caesar as Lewis & Short quotes them. Comenius is post-classical (stapēs, stirrup, is a modern word).
